-   Organizing your workspace
-   Finding and downloading data
-   Importing data in R

:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
In this module we're going to start out with organizing our workspace, followed by finding and downloading data and then getting that data imported into R so that we can actually do something with it.

All of this we want to do with the intent of keeping our analysis reproducible so that when we work with collaborators they can reproduce what we've done. Our most important collaborator, of course, is us, in the future, when we're coming back to something after a few months and need to be able to reproduce what *we* did.
:::

## Introduction

::: {.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
Typically, an analysis project begins with dataset files, a handful of R scripts and output files in a directory. As the project advances, complexity inevitably rises with the addition of more scripts, output files, and possibly new datasets.

The complexity is further amplified when dealing with multiple versions of scripts and output files, necessitating efficient organisation. If these are not well-managed from the beginning, resuming the project after a break, or sharing the project with someone else becomes challenging and time-consuming, as we struggle to recall the project’s status and navigate the directory tree.

Additionally, without proper organization, the project’s complexity could lead to frequent use of the `setwd` function in R to switch between different working directories, resulting in a disorganized workspace.

In this module, we will first focus on an effective strategy for managing the files, both used and generated by our data analysis project, within a working directory.
:::

## Repository structure

::: {.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
For a more streamlined workflow, I suggest storing all files associated with an analysis in a specific directory, which will serve as your project’s working directory. And what's going to make this even better is if this is actually part of a Git repository that we'll be able to use to version control our code and keep track of changes over time.

In these modules, we'll be starting with four specific directories:
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
-   data: raw data
-   scripts: for storing the scripts we've written for the data analysis
-   documents: for documents related to your analysis
-   output: intermediate or final results generated by the scripts in the `scripts/` directory
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
-   data: This is dedicated to storing raw data.

    -   This folder should ideally only house raw data.
    -   It should *not* be modified unless you receive a new dataset (even then, if you have the storage capacity, you should retain the previous dataset as well in case you need it again in the future).
    -   For RNA-seq data analysis, this directory will typically contain `*.fastq` files and any related metadata files for the experiment.
    -   Also, we do *not* want to push these data to GitHub, so be sure to include this in your .gitignore file.
    -   When we're working on a high-performance cluster or other server, we will often also want to house this data on a different drive entirely and link this to our working directory here with a symbolic link.

-   scripts: is for storing the R scripts we've written and utilized for analyzing the data.

-   documents: is for storing documents related to your analysis, such as a manuscript outline or meeting notes with your team.

-   and output: is for storing intermediate or final results generated by the scripts in the `scripts/` directory.

    -   Importantly, if you carry out data cleaning or pre-processing, the output should ideally be stored in this directory as these no longer represent raw data.
    -   Sometimes I'll use an `intermediate/` directory in addition to the output directory just to keep my final results separate from all the intermediate files

As your project grows in complexity, we may find it necessary to create more directories or sub-directories.

In general, however, these four directories (or something similar) should serve as the foundation of your working directory.
:::

## Download the RNA-seq data

::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
Influenza infection triggers disease in a genetic model of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis [@blackmore_influenza_2017]
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
Lastly, we want to download the RNA-seq data required for the rest of the lesson. The dataset we will be using was generated to investigate the impact upper-respiratory infection on changes in RNA transcription in the cerebellum and spinal cord of mice.

This dataset was produced as part of @blackmore_influenza_2017, titled "Influenza infection triggers disease in a genetic model of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis."

The dataset is available at [Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/), under the accession number [GSE96870](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE96870).

Downloading data from GEO is not super straightforward, and we won't be covering that in this lesson. The Carpentries authors of these materials have made the data available on their GitHub repository for easier access, though, so we can download it directly from there.

> switch to Positron

To download the files, we will use the R function

``` r
download.file
```

Actually let's save this in a download script so we can just document where the data are coming from and make it super clear, when we come back to this at a later point, how we got the data.

> create a new file, `scripts/fetch_data.R`

Also to keep my paths and everything a little bit more portable from one computer to another, and so you can use the exact same code that I'm using, we are going to use the `here` package as well.

``` r
root <- here::here()
```

This will give me a direct path to my root working directory - now wherever I'm running this code, it's going to find where we're working and automatically give us the root directory so that we can find the repository in our code.

Okay now we're ready to download our data with `download.file`.

`download.file` needs at least two parameters: `url` and `destfile`. The `url` parameter is used to specify the address on the internet to download the data from, and the `destfile` parameter indicates where to save the downloaded file and what the downloaded file should be named.

Let’s download one of the four data files needed for the remainder of this lesson. The data file is located at https://github.com/carpentries-incubator/bioc-rnaseq/raw/main/episodes/data/GSE96870_counts_cerebellum.csv.

That is a really long name so I have created a tiny url at https://tinyurl.com/mr2thbsj. For my code I'm going to include the full address just because I want to document that but this tiny URL should make it easier for you to work with.

Let's save the downloaded file in the `data/` folder of our repo directory with the name `GSE96870_counts_cerebellum.csv`.

``` r
download.file(url = "https://tinyurl.com/mr2thbsj",
              destfile = file.path(root, 'data', 'GSE96870_counts_cerebellum.csv'))
```

Now if the use of `here` and `root` was not obvious before, hopefully this is beginning to click with you. We can all use the same file path because we use the `here` package and it's going to find the right place on each of our individual laptops to put that file.

All right I can see the file over here in my data directory, and I usually like to just verify that it got downloaded properly, so I'm going to open up my terminal over here and just look at the head of that file.

Okay cool. That's working.

### Load the data in R

Alright! In the last video, we used R to download 4 files from the internet and saved them on our computer. But we do not have these files loaded into R yet so that we can work with them.

The original experimental design in @blackmore_influenza_2017 was fairly complex:

8 week old male and female C57BL/6 mice were collected at Day 0 (before influenza infection), Day 4 and Day 8 after influenza infection. From each mouse, cerebellum and spinal cord tissues were taken for RNA-seq.

There were originally 4 mice per ‘Sex x Time x Tissue’ group, but a few were lost along the way resulting in a total of 45 samples. For this series, we are going to simplify the analysis by only using the 22 cerebellum samples.

Expression quantification was done using STAR to align to the mouse genome and then counting reads that map to genes. In addition to the counts per gene per sample, we also need information on which sample belongs to which Sex/Time point/and Replicate. And it is helpful to annotate the genes with some extra metadata.

Let’s read in the data files that we downloaded in the last episode and start to explore them:

``` r
root <- here::here()

### load data
counts <- read.csv(file.path(root, 'data', 'GSE96870_counts_cerebellum.csv'))
```

All right we have our counts downloaded here. Let's go ahead and take a look and make sure everything looks the way it should.

``` r
# (in console)
str(counts)
```

Genes are in rows and samples are in columns, so we have counts for 41,786 genes and 22 samples. Looks like the row names are gene symbols and the column names are the GEO sample IDs, which are not very informative for telling us which sample is what.

Next read in the sample annotations. Because samples are in columns in the count matrix, we will name the object `coldata`:

``` r
coldata <- read.csv(file.path(root, 'data', 'GSE96870_coldata_cerebellum.csv'))
```

And let's look at this, too:

``` r
# (in console)
str(coldata)
```

Alright, samples are in rows with the GEO sample IDs as the row names, and we have 10 columns of information. The columns that are the most useful for this workshop are `geo_accession` (GEO sample IDs again), `sex` and `time`.

The counts only have gene symbols. While short and somewhat recognizable to the human brain, they are not always good absolute identifiers for exactly what gene was measured. For this we need additional gene annotations that were provided by the authors.

The `count` and `coldata` files were in comma separated value (`.csv`) format, but we cannot use that for our gene annotation file, because the descriptions can contain commas that would prevent a `.csv` file from being read in correctly.

Instead the gene annotation file is in tab separated value (`.tsv`) format. Likewise, the descriptions can contain the single quote ' (for example 5'), which by default R assumes indicates the beginning of a quoted string. So, we have to use a more generic function `read.delim()` with extra arguments to specify that we have tab-separated data with no quotes used.

We also put in other arguments to specify that the first row contains our column names, the gene symbols that should be our `row.names` are in the 5th column, and that NCBI's species-specific gene ID should be read in as character data even though they look like numbers. You can look up these details on available arguments by simply entering the function name starting with question mark.

``` r
?read.delim
```

Okay let's get reading this somewhat messy data in.

``` r
rowranges <- read.delim(file.path(root, 'data',' GSE96870_rowranges.tsv'), 
                        sep = "\t", 
                        colClasses = c(ENTREZID = "character"),
                        header = TRUE, 
                        quote = "", 
                        row.names = 5)
```

Let's just make sure we got that right.

``` r
str(rowranges)
```

For each of the 41,786 genes, we have the `seqnames` (i.e. chromosome number), `start` and `end` positions, `strand`, `ENTREZID`, gene product description (`product`) and the feature type (`gbkey`). These gene-level metadata are useful for the downstream analysis. For example, from the gbkey column, we can check what types of genes and how many of them are in our dataset:

``` r
table(rowranges$gbkey)
```

This brings us to our next challenge.

### SummarizedExperiment objects

![SummarizedExperiment structure](/assets/02_SE.svg)

::: {.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
You can see how keeping related information in separate objects could easily lead to mismatches between our counts, gene annotations and sample annotations. This is why Bioconductor has created a specialized S4 class called a `SummarizedExperiment`.

Let’s take a look at the figure here, representing the anatomy of the `SummarizedExperiment` class.

It is designed to hold any type of quantitative 'omics data here in these `assays` layers, along with linked sample annotations in `colData` and feature annotations in `rowRanges`, with `start` and `stop` positions - or you can just go with a chromosome number/position in `rowData`.

Once these three tables are correctly linked, subsetting either samples and/or features will correctly subset the `assay`, `colData` and `rowRanges` simultaneously.

Additionally, most Bioconductor packages are built around the same core data infrastructure, so they will recognize and be able to manipulate `SummarizedExperiment` objects.

Two of the most popular RNA-seq statistical analysis packages have their own extended S4 classes similar to a `SummarizedExperiment` with additional slots for statistical results: `DESeqDataSet` from `DESeq2` and `DGEList` from `edgeR`. No matter which one you end up using for statistical analysis, you can start by putting your data in a `SummarizedExperiment` object.

### Assemble SummarizedExperiment

> switch to Positron

We'll create a `SummarizedExperiment` from these objects:

-   `count` will be saved in the `assays` slot
-   `coldata`, with sample information, will be stored in `colData` slot - this has our sample metadata, and
-   `rowranges`, describing the genes, will be stored in `rowRanges` slot - this has our feature metadata

Before we put them together, you *really* need to make sure the samples and genes are in the same order! Even though we saw that `count` and `coldata` had the same number of samples and `count` and `rowranges` had the same number of genes, we never explicitly checked to see if they were in the same order.

We can do a quick check of this with

``` r
# (in our script - should be part of the formal record)
### Check data

stopifnot(all.equal(colnames(counts), rownames(coldata)))
stopifnot(all.equal(rownames(counts), rownames(rowranges)))
```

This is going to throw an error in our code if for any reason we end up getting these mixed up.

And if they aren't in the right order we can fix that quickly and easily - let's just add this directly into our code.

``` r
if(!all.equal(colnames(counts), rownames(coldata)))
{
    tempindex <- match(colnames(counts), rownames(coldata))
    coldata <- coldata[tempindex, ]

    # if this is still not true we have bigger problems
    stopifnot(all.equal(colnames(counts), rownames(coldata)))
}
```

Now with this example, we come to our next challenge. \> switch to slides
:::

#### Challenge: Fixing disordered data

If we fix mismatches between `counts` and `coldata` with

``` r
tempindex <- match(colnames(counts), rownames(coldata))
coldata <- coldata[tempindex, ]
```

How would we fix mismatches in the features (i.e. genes) in the assay (e.g. counts) and the gene annotation table (e.g. rowranges)?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
Figure out the code that you would need and we'll be back in the next video with some discussion.

> cut to next video

Okay welcome back. We have an example of matching up our metadata if the column data or the sample metadata is not sorted properly. How are we going to do this if the feature metadata or the row metadata is not matched up properly?

We just need to make some very small changes to this code.

> switch to Positron

``` r
if(!all.equal(rownames(counts), rownames(rowranges)))
{
    tempindex <- match(rownames(counts), rownames(rowranges))
    rowranges <- rowranges[tempindex, ]

    # if this is still not true we have bigger problems
    stopifnot(all.equal(rownames(counts), rownames(rowranges)))
}
```

Once we have verified that samples and genes are in the same order, we can then create our `SummarizedExperiment` object!

``` r
### Create SE object

se <- SummarizedExperiment(
    assays = list(counts = as.matrix(counts)),
    rowRanges = as(rowranges, "GRanges"),
    colData = coldata
)
```

Because matching the genes and samples is so important, the `SummarizedExperiment()` constructor does some internal checks to make sure they contain the same number of genes/samples and the sample/row names match. If not, you will get some error messages:

``` r
# wrong number of samples:
SummarizedExperiment(
    assays = list(counts = as.matrix(counts)),
    rowRanges = as(rowranges, "GRanges"),
    colData = coldata[1:3,]
)

# same number of genes but in different order:
SummarizedExperiment(
  assays = list(counts = as.matrix(counts)),
  rowRanges = as(rowranges[c(2:nrow(rowranges), 1),], "GRanges"),
  colData = coldata
)
```

Let's quickly review how to access the data in `se`.

### Accessing assay data

``` r
# Access the counts
head(assay(se))
dim(assay(se))
```

This works because we only have one layer in that assay slot. If we had more than one assay we could just specify it with the name of the assay that we want.

``` r
head(assay(se, 'counts'))
```

### Accessing sample annotations

``` r
# Access the sample annotations
colData(se)
dim(colData(se))
```

### Accessing gene annotations

``` r
# Access the gene annotations
head(rowData(se))
dim(rowData(se))
```

Now if we wanted to make a single label that had the mouse, sex, and time and mouse id, we could do that with

``` r
# (in script)
# more descriptive sample label
se$Label <- paste(se$sex, se$time, se$mouse, sep = "_")

# (in console)
se$Label
```

Then we can use this label for our column names.

``` r
colnames(se) <- se$Label
```

Now looking at the output here, we can see that they are not in any particular order with respect to sex and time. What if we wanted to fix that?

``` r
# Order samples based on sex and time
se$Group <- paste(se$sex, se$time, sep = "_")

# (in console)
se$Group

# (in script)
se$Group <- factor(se$Group, levels = c("Female_Day0","Male_Day0", 
                                        "Female_Day4","Male_Day4",
                                        "Female_Day8","Male_Day8"))
se <- se[, order(se$Group)]

# (in console)
colData(se)
```

We can also use the same factor formatting to help our figures look a little bit nicer.

``` r
# set Labels as ordered factor
se$Label <- factor(se$Label, levels = se$Label)
```

> cut to next video

Welcome back!

How many samples do we have for each level of the infection variable? ...answer this...

And how many samples represent female mice infected with influenza A on day 8? ...answer this...

Now to illustrate how nice it is to work with these summarized experiment objects, let's go ahead and try something a little bit more complicated. Let's say we want to calculate the mean expression levels of the first 500 genes for the infected group and for the non-infected group separately.

...do that...

``` r
# solution
se_infected <- se[, se$infection == "InfluenzaA"]
se_noninfected <- se[, se$infection == "NonInfected"]

means_infected <- rowMeans(assay(se_infected)[1:500, ])
means_noninfected <- rowMeans(assay(se_noninfected)[1:500, ])

summary(means_infected)
summary(means_noninfected)
```

All right, this wasn't too bad, but if we are working with a *really* large dataset, you can imagine that this process of creating our `SummarizedExperiment` object is going to take some time. If we need to restart R or decide we want to go back and create a new figure or something, then we may not want to have to go through this process of creating the `SummarizedExperiment` object from scratch over and over again.

Let's go ahead and save a copy of it that we can reference in the future. I'm going to save this in my `data/` directory because we haven't really made any changes to it. This is still pretty raw, so that's where I'm going to save it.

``` r
### Save SE object
saveRDS(se, file.path(root, 'data', 'GSE96870_se.rds'))
```

Now if something happens, if I restart R or come back next week or something, I can just pull it up very easily.

> restart R

``` r
se <- readRDS(file.path(root, 'data', 'GSE96870_se.rds'))
```

And we're off and away!

## References
